_why: Child-facing facts for new Toy Piano play-along songs. The owner approved the complete set on 2026-10-20 after independent fact-checking; five corrected facts use new v2 clips so the paid 2026-10-19 renders remain untouched.

yankee-doodle.text: British officers first sang this tune to tease the American colonists. The Americans liked it so much that they sang it too.

sources.claim: British officers sang it to mock colonial soldiers; Americans adopted it

humpty-dumpty.text: Humpty Dumpty was first printed in 1797, probably as a riddle. The answer is an egg, though the rhyme never says so.

sources.claim: earliest printed version 1797; probably a riddle; the rhyme never names an egg

hickory-dickory-dock.text: This rhyme was first printed in 1744. Back then it was spelled ‘Hickere, Dickere Dock.’

sources.claim: first appeared in Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book, London, 1744, spelled Hickere, Dickere Dock

jack-and-jill.text: Jack and Jill was first printed around 1765, and back then the girl’s name was spelled ‘Gill.’

sources.claim: earliest known version in a reprint of Newbery's Mother Goose's Melody (c.1765) spells it Gill

good-king-wenceslas.text: Wenceslas was a real duke of Bohemia, more than a thousand years ago. John Mason Neale wrote this carol about him in 1853.

sources.claim: Wenceslas duke of Bohemia 907-935; Neale wrote the words in 1853

away-in-a-manger.text: This carol was first printed in America in the 1880s. People used to say Martin Luther wrote it, but he did not.

sources.claim: American print appearances in the 1880s; the attribution to Martin Luther is unsupported

au-clair-de-la-lune.text: In 1860, a machine recorded someone singing this song. It is the earliest recognizable recording of a human voice.

sources.claim: phonautograph recording by Scott de Martinville, 9 April 1860: earliest recognizable record of the human voice

sur-le-pont-d-avignon.text: Floods broke much of the Avignon bridge long ago. Only four of its twenty-two arches are left standing.

sources.claim: Pont Saint-Benezet: 22 arches originally, four remain; arches collapsed in floods

pat-a-cake.text: Pat-a-Cake is more than three hundred years old. It was first written down in a play in 1698.

sources.claim: earliest recorded version in D'Urfey's The Campaigners, 1698

o-come-all-ye-faithful.text: This carol was first printed in Latin in 1751, as ‘Adeste Fideles.’ Frederick Oakeley made the English words in 1841.

sources.claim: earliest printed version 1751 in Wade's Cantus Diversi; Oakeley translated 1841

hark-the-herald.text: Charles Wesley wrote these words in 1739. A tune adapted from Mendelssohn’s music was added in 1855.

sources.claim: Wesley's Hymn for Christmas-Day 1739; Cummings adapted Mendelssohn's Festgesang 1855

in-the-bleak-midwinter.text: Christina Rossetti’s poem was printed in 1872. Gustav Holst’s tune for it came in 1906.

sources.claim: poem published Jan 1872; Holst's Cranham published 1906 in The English Hymnal

the-holly-and-the-ivy.text: Cecil Sharp wrote this carol down in 1909, after hearing Mary Clayton sing it in an English town.

sources.claim: Sharp noted the tune from Mary Clayton in Chipping Campden, 1909

can-can.text: Jacques Offenbach wrote this tune for a comic opera in 1858. Later it became the music for the can-can dance.

sources.claim: Orphee aux enfers premiered 21 Oct 1858; Galop infernal later used for the can-can

minuet-in-g.text: People once thought Bach wrote this, but it was by Christian Petzold. It was in Anna Magdalena Bach’s notebook in 1725.

sources.claim: in Notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach dated 1725; now attributed to Petzold

once-in-royal-davids-city.text: Cecil Frances Alexander wrote these words in 1848, in a book of hymns for little children.

sources.claim: first published 1848 in Hymns for Little Children

der-mond-ist-aufgegangen.text: Matthias Claudius wrote this poem in 1779. Johann Schulz wrote a tune for it in 1790.

sources.claim: poem in Musen-Almanach 1779; Schulz melody published 1790

mary-had-a-little-lamb.text: Mary Had a Little Lamb was printed in 1830, and Sarah Josepha Hale is usually named as its author. In 1877, Thomas Edison used it to test his new phonograph.

sources.claim: printed in 1830; Hale is usually credited amid a disputed authorship; Edison recited it in his 1877 phonograph test

three-blind-mice.text: Three Blind Mice was printed in 1609, over four hundred years ago, as a round for three voices.

sources.claim: earliest known publication 1609, Ravenscroft's Deuteromelia, three-voice round

deck-the-hall.text: This tune is from an old Welsh New Year’s Eve carol. Thomas Oliphant wrote the English words in 1862.

sources.claim: tune from Welsh carol Nos Galan; Oliphant's English words first published 1862

canon-in-d.text: Pachelbel wrote this canon more than three hundred years ago, but it became famous only after a 1968 recording.

sources.claim: composed between about 1680 and 1706; obscure until a 1968 recording

fur-elise.text: Für Elise was not printed until 1867, forty years after Beethoven died.

sources.claim: published 1867, 40 years after Beethoven's death

brahms-lullaby.text: Brahms wrote this lullaby in 1868 for his friend Bertha Faber, to celebrate the birth of her baby.

sources.claim: published Nov 1868, dedicated to Bertha Faber for the birth of her second son

eine-kleine-nachtmusik.text: Mozart finished this piece in Vienna in 1787. Its name means ‘a little night music.’

sources.claim: completed Vienna 10 Aug 1787; title translates 'a little night music'

morning-mood.text: Grieg wrote this music for a play in 1875. It paints a sunrise over the desert in Morocco.

sources.claim: written 1875 for Ibsen's Peer Gynt; depicts a sunrise in the Moroccan desert

entertainer.text: Scott Joplin published this piano rag in 1902. It became famous again in 1973 in a film called The Sting.

sources.claim: published 1902 by John Stark & Son; theme of The Sting (1973)

swan-lake.text: Tchaikovsky’s ballet Swan Lake was first performed in Moscow in 1877.

sources.claim: premiere 1877 at the Bolshoi Theatre, Moscow

london-bridge.text: London Bridge is Falling Down was first printed with its words around 1744, in a book of songs.

sources.claim: earliest printed version with words c.1744, Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book

rock-a-bye-baby.text: Rock-a-bye Baby was in a book called Mother Goose’s Melody, printed in London around 1765.

sources.claim: earliest known printing Mother Goose's Melody, London, c.1765

jolly-good-fellow.text: The tune of this song comes from an old French song, ‘Marlborough Has Left for the War.’

sources.claim: tune from French 'Malbrough s'en va-t-en guerre', at least 18th century

nkosi-sikelel-iafrika.text: Enoch Sontonga, a teacher, wrote this hymn in 1897. Part of it is in South Africa’s national anthem today.

sources.claim: composed 1897 by Enoch Sontonga; 1997 anthem includes parts of it

joy-to-world.text: Isaac Watts wrote the words to Joy to the World in 1719. Lowell Mason arranged the tune in the 1830s.

sources.claim: Watts published the words in 1719; Mason's arrangement appeared in the 1830s

first-noel.text: The First Noel probably comes from Cornwall in England. Its words were first printed in 1823.

sources.claim: probable Cornish origin; Davies Gilbert first printed the words in 1823

when-saints-go-marching.text: When the Saints Go Marching In is a spiritual that is traditionally played at jazz funerals in New Orleans.

sources.claim: African-American spiritual; traditionally performed at New Orleans jazz funerals

old-macdonald.text: An early version of this song was printed in 1706, in a show by Thomas d'Urfey.

sources.claim: a farm-animal-sound ancestor appeared in Thomas d'Urfey's 1706 show The Kingdom of the Birds

oh-where-has-my-little-dog-gone.text: Septimus Winner wrote this song in 1864, and he set it to an old German folk tune.

sources.claim: written by Septimus Winner 1864; set to German folk tune
